analysis.one_liner: Opens federal lands and offshore areas to oil drilling, suspends federal gas taxes above $3 a gallon, and gives refiners tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill attracted no cosponsors, was referred to three committees, and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have rolled back federal restrictions on offshore oil and gas drilling and opened the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to drilling. It would have automatically suspended the federal gasoline tax whenever the nationwide average pump price topped $3.00 a gallon, made it harder to sue over federal environmental reviews of drilling and refinery projects, and given oil refiners bigger tax write-offs for building new refineries. It was introduced by Rep. Ron Paul, drew no cosponsors, and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers and truckers would pay less at the pump when prices spike, since the federal fuel tax (about 18.4 cents per gallon) would be suspended and mileage deductions would rise. Oil and gas companies would gain the most in the long run: expanded access to offshore areas and the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, bigger tax write-offs for refinery construction, and a shield against lawsuits over environmental reviews. Refiners would get immediate tax benefits.

how_it_helps.text: It lifts federal restrictions on offshore drilling and on drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, aiming to increase oil supply and eventually lower prices [S2, S3].
It suspends the 18.4-cent federal gasoline tax automatically whenever retail gas exceeds $3.00 a gallon, immediately cutting what drivers pay at the pump during price spikes [S2, S3].

It raises the deductible mileage rate for business driving to at least 70 cents per mile, and during tax-suspension periods lets medical, moving, and charitable driving be deducted at that same rate [S3].
It gives oil companies bigger tax write-offs for building refineries and blocks lawsuits that challenge federal environmental-impact statements, to make new refineries easier to build [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Federal fuel taxes fund highways and transit; every suspension period would force the Treasury to backfill trust funds from general revenue, adding to deficits. Removing environmental judicial review shifts risk of drilling and refinery harms onto communities near those projects. Refinery tax breaks are a cost borne by other taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Suspending federal fuel taxes whenever gas tops $3.00 a gallon would cut off the dedicated funding for highway and transit trust funds, forcing general Treasury money to cover it [S3].
Making federal environmental-impact statements immune to judicial review would eliminate citizens' and communities' ability to challenge projects like drilling and refineries in court [S3].

Opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain and the Outer Continental Shelf to drilling carries well-understood risks to fragile ecosystems and coastal economies, and any price effect would come years later [S3].
New tax write-offs for refinery construction are subsidies to large oil refiners, and there is no guarantee savings would reach consumers rather than shareholders [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For drivers, the most tangible piece—the gas tax holiday—would save money at the pump when prices spike, but it would drain road and transit funding and hand the difference to consumers and fuel sellers only if stations passed the cut through. The supply-side pieces aim at prices through a years-long process, and achieve it partly by making it harder to challenge projects in court, a real cost in environmental protection. The refineries would get valuable new tax write-offs on the public's tab. On balance, this was a statement bill favoring energy producers; nothing in it came close to enactment.

outcome.mechanism: Nobody else in Congress signed on, the bill sat in three House committees without a hearing or vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Ron Paul introduced the bill on May 21, 2009; no other member cosponsored it [S1, S4].
It was referred the same day to the Ways and Means, Natural Resources, and Financial Services committees, and in June 2009 to a Natural Resources subcommittee [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and refiners are better off because the bill died, since it would have handed them expanded drilling access and new tax breaks; environmental review and fuel-tax funding also survived intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas producers and refiners

for.name: Rep. Ron Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it was referred to three committees.

against.name: House Ways and Means, Natural Resources, and Financial Services Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral—no hearing, markup, or vote—letting the bill die.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split ever formed.

industries.note: The bill removes federal restrictions on offshore leasing and opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to drilling, expanding where producers can develop reserves, and shields federal environmental reviews from court challenges.
Refiners would get 100% expensing and favorable 5-year depreciation for new refinery construction—substantial tax subsidies that lower their cost of building capacity.

Drivers would pay less at the pump during price spikes (tax suspension, higher mileage deductions) but the highway trust fund would have to be backfilled from general revenue, and the long-term price benefit from drilling is speculative.
By making environmental-impact statements unreviewable in court, the bill removes the main legal tool citizens use to challenge drilling and refinery projects.
